title: This Fish Snipes Bugs From 3 Meters Away 🎯
description:
How does an archerfish shoot bugs off leaves with a jet of water? It presses its tongue into a groove in the roof of its mouth to make a tube, then snaps its gill covers shut to fire a water jet that can hit insects 2-3 meters away.

Sources:
https://australian.museum/learn/animals/fishes/banded-archerfish-toxotes-jaculatrix/
https://denverzoo.org/animals/archerfish/
https://phys.org/news/2013-12-uncover-amazing-physics-feat-archerfish.html

Animated in the Flat-Vector Science style.

topic: How does an archerfish shoot bugs out of the air?
script:
Could you spit a bug off a leaf 3 meters away?
This fish can.
It's called the archerfish.
It hides just under the surface,
and spots a bug sitting on a leaf above.
It doesn't jump. It spits.
So how does that work?
It presses its tongue against a groove in the roof of its mouth.
That makes a tiny tube, like a gun barrel.
Then it snaps its gill covers shut,
and water blasts out of that tube.
And here's the clever part.
The back of the jet moves faster than the front,
so the water bunches into one big blob,
right before it hits.
Big archerfish can hit a bug two to three meters away.
Smack! The bug drops,
and dinner falls right into the water.
So be honest.
How far do you think you could spit?
key_facts: Archerfish press the tongue against a groove in the roof of the mouth, forming a tube (Denver Zoo, Australian Museum)
Closing the gill covers forces water out through the tube (Australian Museum)
The rear of the jet moves faster than the front, so water gathers into a big drop just before impact (Vailati et al. 2012, via phys.org)
Large archerfish can hit targets 2-3 m away (Australian Museum)
